node-2.label: 37-year-old Japanese man underwent imaging which revealed a 10 mm cystic lesion with a mural nodule near the anterior horn of the right lateral ventricle

node-3.label: Despite the absence of neurological symptoms, the patient was monitored over a period of 10 years

node-4.label: During this time, the lesion increased in size from 10 mm to 18 mm

attrs.why: The radiologist and pathologist now both favor a low-grade glioneuronal tumor (likely ganglioglioma) as the cause of the worsening headaches, with supporting imaging features (Gd-enhancing mural nodule, T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, T2* hypointensity) and 10-year growth. Because no primary headache or alternative explanation is supported, confidence rises from 0.75 to 0.85.

Both experts reiterate that obstructive hydrocephalus is anatomically plausible given the lesion's proximity to the foramen of Monro, but they explicitly state it remains unconfirmed because ventricular size and CSF data are unavailable. No new evidence confirms ventriculomegaly, so confidence remains 0.55.

The radiologist and pathologist strongly argue against a primary headache disorder, emphasizing the structural lesion, enhancing mural nodule, abnormal T2* signal, and interval growth. This additional expert consensus lowers confidence from 0.15 to 0.05.
